anchor: When icicles hang by the wall
title: The song of Winter
short: The owl's song of Hiems (Winter), which with the cuckoo's song of Ver (Spring) ends Love's Labour's Lost; Palgrave titled it 'Winter'.
body: Love's Labour's Lost (c. 1595) ends not with the expected weddings but with a year's postponement, and Armado introduces a debate in song between Ver, the spring, 'maintained by the Cuckoo', and Hiems, the winter, 'maintained by the Owl'. This is the winter song. Armado closes the play: 'The words of Mercury are harsh after the songs of Apollo.' The homely English winter scene contrasts with the play's courtly wit, and many critics see the songs as returning the play to the real seasons and duties the lords must now face. Palgrave printed it as 'Winter' in The Golden Treasury.

title: blows his nail
short: Blows on his fingers to warm them; the phrase also meant to wait idly.
body: Literally, the shepherd blows on his fingernails to warm his hands. 'To blow one's nails' was also an idiom for waiting patiently with nothing to do; compare 3 Henry VI 2.5.3, where the shepherd 'blowing of his nails' cannot tell whether it is day or night. Dick, Tom, Joan and Marian are typical English rustic names, giving the song its village cast.

anchor: milk comes frozen home in pail
title: milk comes frozen home in pail
short: Milk freezes in the pail on the way back from milking: a precise, unadorned detail of rural winter.
body: The detail is realistic rather than conventional and contributes to the song's admired particularity. Unlike the pastoral idealisation common in Elizabethan verse, the scene is cold, domestic and working. Critics often cite this song as an example of Shakespeare's plain English realism. The plain monosyllables and run of 'and' clauses give the song the feel of a ballad or folk-song. The milkmaid's work outdoors is set against the kitchen work within, both part of the shared household economy.

title: When blood is nipt, and ways be foul
short: When the blood is chilled by frost, and roads are muddy and impassable.
body: 'Nipt' (nipped) means pinched with cold, frostbitten; the Elizabethans thought cold literally congealed the blood. 'Ways be foul' means the roads are deep in mud, a real hardship of winter travel before paved roads. The subjunctive 'be' is a normal Elizabethan form after 'when'. The idea of cold blood connects with Galenic medicine, in which winter was the cold and moist season, ruled by phlegm. The 'nipping' cold recurs in Shakespeare (Hamlet 1.4, 'a nipping and an eager air').

title: the staring owl
short: The wide-eyed owl, bird of winter night; its call, ominous in other contexts, is here 'a merry note'.
body: 'Staring' describes the owl's large fixed eyes. The owl was normally a bird of ill omen (compare Macbeth 2.2), and in the companion spring song the cuckoo's call is 'unpleasing to a married ear' because it mocks cuckolds. The inversion is witty: the spring bird threatens, while the winter owl sings 'a merry note', because the winter scene is one of shared domestic comfort.

title: Tu-whit, tu-whoo
short: The owl's cry forms the refrain, onomatopoeic and shortened in line length, ending each stanza with the kitchen scene.
body: The refrain imitates the owl's call; 'tu-whit, tu-whoo' combines the female tawny owl's 'kewick' and the male's hoot. The short lines break the four-stress pattern of the stanza and imitate the bird's rhythm. The refrain's final line returns each time to 'greasy Joan' at the pot, so that the cold outdoors is always answered by the warm kitchen. The final line of the stanza returns to the hearth, linking the owl's cry with the comfort of shared food.

title: greasy Joan
short: A kitchen maid, greasy from cooking; 'Joan' was a typical name for a country girl or servant.
body: 'Joan' was the stock name of a rustic woman or servant (compare the proverb 'Joan is as good as my lady in the dark', and Berowne's 'some men must love my lady, and some Joan' in this play, 3.1). 'Greasy' is affectionately literal: she is sweaty and spattered from cooking. Her presence at the fire anchors the song in domestic labour.

title: keel the pot
short: To cool the pot by stirring, skimming or adding cold liquid, so that it does not boil over.
body: 'Keel' derives from Old English celan, to cool. To 'keel the pot' was to prevent it from boiling over, by stirring, skimming or pouring in a little cold water. The verb survived in northern dialect. The detail completes the realistic kitchen scene that answers the frozen world outside. Some modern writers have taken it as a brewer's term for a cooling vat, but the OED sense of cooling is standard.

title: the parson's saw
short: The parson's maxim or sermon, drowned out by the congregation's coughing.
body: A 'saw' is a saying or moral maxim (Old English sagu), here the parson's sententious sermon. Winter coughing in the cold church drowns it out, a gently comic touch at the expense of the clergy. Compare Jaques's justice 'full of wise saws and modern instances' (As You Like It 2.7). The comedy is gentle but social: the sermon is lost in the noise of a cold congregation, much as the play's own wit is lost in the final reckoning of winter.

title: Dick ... Tom ... Marian
short: Common English village names, giving the scene a particular community; Marian's raw red nose is comic and realistic.
body: Dick, Tom, Joan and Marian are generic English rustic names; 'Maid Marian' was also a figure of the May games, which may give the winter scene an ironic echo of spring festivity. The comic close-up of 'Marian's nose' looking 'red and raw' with cold is typical of the song's affectionate realism. The names were common enough among English villagers to need no further identification, and the song invites the audience to recognise neighbours.

anchor: roasted crabs hiss in the bowl
title: roasted crabs
short: Roasted crab-apples hissing as they are dropped into a bowl of hot spiced ale, a winter drink.
body: 'Crabs' are crab-apples, roasted and then put into hot ale, often spiced and sugared (a drink later called 'lambswool'). They 'hiss' as they meet the liquid. Puck in A Midsummer Night's Dream 2.1 lurks 'in a gossip's bowl / In very likeness of a roasted crab'. The image of festive warmth contrasts with the 'birds brooding in the snow'. The roasted apples were also used in wassail.
